title: TC3-02596
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): He appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) is a citizen of Mexico. He appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.

I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The Appellant fears harm by the Plague Number 7 gang in Mexico because he refused to work with them.

The Appellant's allegations are as follows. The Appellant is from Queretaro, Mexico. When he was a teenager, the Plague Number 7 gang approached the Appellant and his friend to sell drugs for them. The Appellant refused, but his friend agreed and was later shot and killed by the gang. In 2002 or 2003, the Appellant was on a bus when two people threatened him with a knife to give them his phone. In 2005 or 2006, the Appellant and his parents were robbed at gunpoint. The Appellant began to experience paranoia and anxiety.

In XXXX 2014, the Appellant went to Spain for six months. In 2015, after he returned to Mexico, he was robbed while walking on the street. In XXXX 2020, the Appellant left Mexico to study in Canada. In January 2022, the Appellant filed a refugee claim.
The RPD rejected the claim based on an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Merida, Yucatan. The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in its IFA assessment.
The Appellant does not request to submit new evidence on appeal. As there is no new evidence admitted on appeal, there can be no oral hearing pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.
paragraphs.heading_before: NO NEW EVIDENCE, NO ORAL HEARING

paragraphs.text: My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1 I find that the RPD correctly determined that the Appellant has an IFA in Merida. There is no nexus
The RPD found that there was no evidence to indicate that the alleged criminal acts were motivated by reason of a Convention ground, and therefore assessed the claim under section 96 of the IRPA.
The Appellant does not contest this finding on appeal.

After my independent assessment, I find that the RPD properly determined that the Appellant's claim has no nexus to a Convention ground and have assessed this appeal pursuant to subsection 97(1) of the IRPA. Credibility Adverse inference from omission of identity of agent of harm
The RPD drew an adverse inference from an omission in the Appellant's Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative regarding the identity of the agents of harm in the 2015 attack.

The Appellant submits that, at the hearing, when asked about his failure to reference in his narrative some details provided in his testimony, he responded that his mental condition and trauma he experienced rendered him unwilling and/or unable to recall the details at the time of preparing the narrative. The Appellant challenges the RPD finding that this response was not credible. He states that he has been receiving XXXX in Mexico and Canada and has been diagnosed with XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX) that include intrusive memories from trauma and decreased levels of concentration. The Appellant submits that this condition played a role in his omission of some details of the traumatic incidents.

I find that the RPD did not err in drawing an adverse inference from the Appellant omitting from his BOC narrative reference to the identity of the agent of harm in the 2015 attack. I find that the evidence does not establish on a balance of probabilities that the Plague Number 7 gang were involved in the 2015 attack.

I have reviewed the Appellant's BOC narrative after which I agree with the RPD that the Appellant omits reference to a particular agent of harm regarding the 2015 attack. The Appellant's BOC narrative describes the 2015 attack as follows: ...one day when I was back to Mexico and was walking on the street, a person asked me for money. I made a mistake and stopped to listen to what he was asking for and then I found myself surrounded by four guys that had appeared out of thin air. They punched me in the stomach and tried to drag me to a car parked nearby but I resisted and fought back and ran as fast as I could until I found a crowded place and mixed in with other people, totally out of breath and traumatized.2

The Appellant's BOC narrative reads as if this was a random attempted robbery. He makes no reference to the identity of the people who attacked him or the Plague Number 7 gang. However, the Appellant refers to the involvement of the Plague Number 7 gang in his description of the first two incidents. I also note that the Appellant testified that the first incident occurred in 2002 or 20033 and the second incident occurred in 2005 or 2006.4 Therefore, the 2015 attack occurred 9 to 10 years after the second incident.

At the hearing, after the Appellant explained what happened during the 2015 attack, the RPD asked him how he knew that it was the Plague Number 7 gang who attacked him, to which he responded: Because they call each other one more time, perro and they were clear to send a message to me that they knew that I was back. I am going to say in Spanish, sorry. They knew that I had come back because they were once again calling each other perros or dogs and when they referred to me saying that they knew that I had come back, they specified that they came from the Plague Seven and they continued to insult me and trying to hit me.5

The RPD asked the Appellant why he did not state in his BOC narrative that they specified that they were from the Plague Number 7 gang, to which he responded: As I mentioned, those are traumas. Sometimes I prefer always to keep it in general, and it's sometimes it's very difficult to talk about that, even right now, I am trying to be calm about that. I feel that my voice is a little shattered. So it is very difficult to talk about that. It's not something like easy, because not everybody can say that oh, I have a gun in my face. My mother has a gun in my face, and my father also, so for sure, it is difficult. If they try to beat you, if they try to kill you three (3) times in your whole life and they threaten you every, every time, you get tired and tired and tired and for sure, the only thing that you want to do is forget those things to live your life so that's the reason why it's difficult sometimes to remember all those things.6

I find the Appellant's explanation that he prefers to speak generally and that it is difficult to talk about and remember everything fails to reasonably explain him omitting the identity of his attackers in his BOC narrative. While I accept that it may be difficult for the Appellant to recount these experiences or to remember details, the identity of his attackers is significant and he testified that they told him who they were. Further, as noted above, the Appellant identified his attackers in his description of the previous two incidents in his BOC narrative. I also note that the Appellant was represented by counsel since the time that he signed his BOC narrative. Even if the Appellant did not remember to include the identity of his attackers at the time he completed his narrative, he could have made an amendment to his narrative prior to the hearing. Insufficient evidence of ongoing threats

The RPD found that the Appellant did not credibly establish that his agents of harm have continued to seek out his family since he arrived in Canada in XXXX 2020. The Appellant testified that his father told him in XXXX or XXXX 2021 that he was being threatened recently and constantly but that he did not have anything to corroborate this because his father told him this and does not know how to use technology. The RPD did not accept this explanation as credible as the Appellant did not note this in his narrative which he signed in January 2022. Further, the Appellant provided a letter from his father and mother which contains no indication that the agents of harm have continued to pursue them recently and constantly.

The Appellant submits that he mentioned the ongoing pursuit by his agents of harm in his narrative and that it is implied when he provided evidence and disclosure to the RPD. The Appellant submits that him trying to prove the continuity of the risk through evidence from the very beginning shows the credibility of his later claims of the existence of such risks. The Appellant submits that the presumption of truth applies and that, given that he was found credible regarding his identity and education, it is reasonable to infer his credibility regarding his fear in Mexico.

The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in finding that he did not note the ongoing threats in his narrative despite testifying to it at the hearing. The Appellant references a portion of his narrative in which he refers to his aunt calling him a month before he signed his BOC form to tell him that his father was being threatened for his whereabouts. The Appellant submits that this is clear indication of his family's report on the ongoing harassment and threats from the agents of harm that continued even after he left Mexico and arrived in Canada.
The Appellant submits that the ongoing harassment and threats of the agents of harm can be derived from his father's letter.

I find that the RPD correctly determined that the Appellant did not credibly establish that his agents of harm have continued to seek out his family since he arrived in Canada in XXXX 2020. I have reviewed the RPD record, including the transcript of the hearing, as part of my independent assessment. At the hearing, the Appellant testified that, in XXXX or XXXX 2021, his father told him that people repeatedly marked his house and asked about the Appellant. The Appellant testified that this was occurring recently and constantly.7 However, the Appellant does not refer to his father telling him this in his BOC narrative.

In his BOC narrative, the Appellant states the following: But things were not as easy as I thought. My aunt called about a month ago and told that my father was being threatened by some "weird guys" who were searching for me and asking about my number and address. My family refused to give away any information, but they were worried about me.8
As the Appellant's BOC form was signed in January 2022, the Appellant received this call from his aunt around XXXX 2021.

I acknowledge the Appellant's submission that his BOC narrative refers to his father being threatened after he left Mexico. However, the Appellant's BOC narrative and testimony are inconsistent regarding how the Appellant learned of the ongoing threats. While the Appellant refers to his aunt informing him of the threats in his BOC narrative, he does not refer to this in his testimony. Rather, in his testimony, the Appellant refers to his father telling him about the ongoing threats but does not refer to this in his narrative.

At the hearing, the RPD asked the Appellant if he had anything from his father to support the ongoing threats, to which he responded that his father has difficulty with technology, that he does not have anything written down as he does not know how to type on the phone, and that his father told him this.9

I disagree with the Appellant's submission that the ongoing harassment and threats of the agents of harm can be derived from his father's letter. The letter states the following: After all this, my son decided that the best thing to do was to study abroad in Canada, but things have become very difficult lately, so I have recommended him to stay, because the robberies, murders and violence have been escalating, I even fear for his safety because the surviving robbers have been growing in terms of criminal level and have become part of organized crime..."10

While this portion of the letter refers to increased criminality and violence, and to the robbers becoming part of organized crime, it does not refer to any specific incidents or threats made against the Appellant or his family.

I fail to see, nor does the Appellant explain, how him trying to prove the continuity of the risk through evidence from the beginning demonstrates the credibility of his later claims of the existence of such risks. Further, while I agree that the presumption of truth applies, I fail to see how the Appellant being found credible regarding his identity and education demonstrates that he is credible regarding the ongoing threats. Rather, I find that the evidence does not establish the ongoing threats on a balance of probabilities. The Appellant has a viable IFA The IFA is safe

The RPD found that the agents of harm are unlikely to pursue the Appellant in Merida. The RPD found it unlikely that the agents of harm would go out of their way to pursue and harm the Appellant in a different part of Mexico three years after he left. The RPD noted that the Appellant's profile would not be of ongoing interest to the agents of harm. Further, the RPD noted that the Appellant failed to establish that his agents of harm had reached out to him since he departed Mexico.

The RPD found that the alleged agents of harm do not have the organizational capacity to locate the Appellant in the IFA location. The RPD noted that the National Documentation Package (NDP) contains no information regarding the Plague Number 7 gang. The RPD found it reasonable to expect that, if an organization was of sufficient strength and reach to be able to learn of a person's return to Mexico, or their presence in any city in Mexico, there would be objective country conditions evidence to support this.
The Appellant submits that, considering that members of his family have been contacted and the agents of harm have looked for him, they have the motivation and ability to find him.

The Appellant submits that a personal vendetta could motivate a gang to track someone outside their area. The Appellant submits that the reputations of gangs depend in part on their ability to make people who refuse to work for them, or comply with them, disappear.

The Appellant submits that the agents of harm have the capacity to locate him as his employment in Mexico would make his contact with criminals more probable. The Appellant submits that gangs and cartels use informants, monitor social media feeds and accounts, or use GPS trackers on cars, in order to track people down. The Appellant submits that gangs use corrupt law enforcement agents to obtain information about people they pursue. The Appellant refers to the documentary evidence demonstrating that organized crime is present throughout Mexico and that he is at risk in any city in Mexico.
The Appellant refers to police corruption and the deterioration of the security situation in Mexico leaving him unable to access adequate state protection.
I find that the RPD correctly determined that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Merida.

Contrary to the Appellant's submission that his agents of harm contacting his family members establishes their motivation and ability to locate him, as outlined above, the evidence does not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that his agents of harm have contacted his family since he left Mexico. As outlined above, the Appellant's evidence was inconsistent regarding the ongoing threats.

I agree with the Appellant that the objective documentary evidence indicates that a personal vendetta, including refusing to work for a gang, could motivate the gang to track someone outside their area. However, considering that the ongoing threats and the involvement of the Plague Number 7 gang in the 2015 attack were not established on a balance of probabilities, the last interaction with the gang was in 2005 or 2006, or over 16 years ago. Considering the length of time that has elapsed, I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the gang is no longer interested in the Appellant.

While I acknowledge that organized crime is present throughout Mexico, this does not result in a personalized risk to the Appellant throughout Mexico. Further, as noted by the RPD, if the Plague Number 7 gang were of sufficient strength and reach to learn of a person's return to Mexico, or their presence in any city in Mexico, the objective country conditions would make reference to it. I reviewed the NDP as part of my independent assessment and was not able to find reference to the Plague Number 7 gang. I find that the objective evidence does not establish that the Plague Number 7 gang have the organizational capacity to locate the Appellant throughout Mexico.
I fail to see, nor does the Appellant explain, how his employment in Mexico would make his contact with criminals more probable.

I find it unnecessary to address the Appellant's submissions regarding his inability to access adequate state protection in Mexico. This decision, and that of the RPD, do not rely on state protection and the finding that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Mexico is determinative. Relocation to the IFA is reasonable
The RPD found that relocation to the IFA is reasonable in the Appellant's circumstances.
The Appellant does not contest this finding on appeal.

After my independent assessment, I find that the RPD correctly determined that relocation to Merida is reasonable in the Appellant's circumstances. The RPD asked the Appellant about any reasons he could not relocate to the IFA locations aside from his fears, to which he replied that he is afraid. The RPD properly considered the Appellant's education and employment experience, and language ability, and found it not unreasonable for him to relocate to Merida.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA. (signed) L.
